comparator.name: Human Resource Studies
comparator.sourceNotes: The adopted 2026–2027 Appendix I confirms the Dutch full-time Personeelwetenschappen track, with 60 EC in each year. The 30 EC mobility window permits combinations of placement, minor and electives. Coaching and Development is the first of two equal professionalisation choices; the English People Management track has a different curriculum.
components: Professional Skills in Human Resource Studies
GROW mentoring and personal development continue across the programme and carry no credits.
Academic Writing in Human Resource Studies A
Social Psychology for the Social Sciences
The ordinary first-year binding study advice threshold is 42 EC.
Academic Writing in Human Resource Studies B
Mobility Window: Minor, Placement or Electives
Choose a combination of placement, minor and/or electives for 30 EC in total, at Tilburg or abroad. The comparison leaves this content open.
Choose one 6 EC course: Coaching and Development or Managing Teams and Social Capital. This example uses the first-listed choice.
The Future of Work: Sustainable and Critical Perspectives
Social Philosophy for Human Resource Studies
Bachelor’s Thesis in Human Resource Studies
Entry to the bachelor thesis requires 120 EC. This pathway earns those credits by the end of year two.

routeSelection.basis: The official detailed curriculum requires one of two 6-ECTS professionalisation electives without identifying either as the general route. Coaching en Ontwikkeling is listed first and is therefore instantiated as a neutral official-order tie-break; the choice was made before and independently of UCR course selection.

core: Human-resource management, strategic personnel policy and the relationship between organisational performance and employee well-being
Psychological and sociological analysis of people, work, organisations and organisational behaviour
Employee well-being, workplace health, stress, development, coaching and assessment
People analytics and evidence-based human-resource research and decisions
Labour relations, employment law and the future of work
adjacent: Teamwork, social capital and employee development in organisational settings
questions: How can organisations balance performance with employee health, development and well-being?
How can research and people analytics support evidence-based personnel decisions?
How do law, technology and changing labour relations reshape the future of employment?

candidates.label: Workplace psychology, well-being and employee development
Labour relations, institutions and the future of work

selection.assessment: The closest option addresses organisational behaviour, evidence-based decisions and strategic and financial context. The second develops psychological health and development; the third develops institutions and policy affecting organisations and work. These are different curricular priorities, with each pair exceeding the four-course floor. No fourth option is considered.

alternatives.label: People, organisations & strategy
alternatives.labelReason: Study how organisations coordinate people and respond to changing work. Combine organisational psychology, leadership, negotiation, social research and finance with economic and digital strategy.
alternatives.concept: Study how organisations coordinate people and respond to changing work. Combine organisational psychology, leadership, negotiation, social research and finance with economic and digital strategy.
progression: Checked all current offerings and formal prerequisites. Research methods precedes negotiation and organisational psychology; introductory economics precedes advanced economics. Brain and behaviour foundations precede health and clinical psychology where selected.

alternatives.label: Psychology, health & people at work
alternatives.labelReason: Study the psychological foundations of behaviour, health, stress and development, and apply social research and leadership to people at work. Business and economic courses provide a complementary organisational setting.
alternatives.concept: Study the psychological foundations of behaviour, health, stress and development, and apply social research and leadership to people at work. Business and economic courses provide a complementary organisational setting.
progression: Checked all current offerings and formal prerequisites. Research methods precedes negotiation and organisational psychology; introductory economics precedes advanced economics. Brain and behaviour foundations precede health and clinical psychology where selected.
alternatives.distinctness: Compared with the first option, this option gives sustained space to psychopathology, health, development, psychological assessment and evidence synthesis, rather than digital strategy, international business and public economics.

alternatives.label: Institutions, policy & organisations
alternatives.labelReason: Study the institutions and policies that shape organisations and economic life. Combine law, political institutions, economics and social inquiry with organisational psychology, negotiation and research.
alternatives.concept: Study the institutions and policies that shape organisations and economic life. Combine law, political institutions, economics and social inquiry with organisational psychology, negotiation and research.
progression: Checked all current offerings and formal prerequisites. Research methods precedes negotiation and organisational psychology; introductory economics precedes advanced economics. Brain and behaviour foundations precede health and clinical psychology where selected.
alternatives.distinctness: This option prioritises political institutions, rights, international and EU law, policy analysis and political economy. The others give more weight to leadership practice or psychological health and development.

courses: Business & Economy in the Age of AI
New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
trace: develops academic writing, research literacy and reflective collaboration as common foundations
interprets financial statements and develops budgeting, costing and investment appraisal
examines AI, workforce change, productivity and inequality to support analysis of technological change in work
introduces incentives, markets and government intervention through economic models
analyses consumer choice, imperfect competition, labour markets and externalities
assesses taxation, public spending and policy through efficiency and equity
assesses how organisations adopt digital tools and plans strategic change
examines governance, trade and responsibility and develops a research-based market-entry strategy
uses design thinking to identify needs and develop a venture concept and prototype
designs empirical studies and uses surveys, sampling and introductory statistics
applies leadership theories, emotional intelligence and reflective planning to group and personal development
analyses leaders’ communication and develops advice from interviews and rhetorical practice
uses a supervised survey project to study emotion regulation, belonging and inclusive leadership
examines behaviour, teams, culture and change and synthesises evidence about organisational practice
uses simulations to study bargaining, power, framing and collaborative decision-making
Compares legal traditions and examines the social and normative roles of law.
uses historical sources to study modern political, economic and cultural transformations
studies human rights through legal instruments, protection systems and philosophical argument
Examines public international law, institutions and relationships with national legal systems.
examines EU law, institutions, citizenship and the relationship between EU and domestic law
develops ethical reasoning about responsibilities and competing values relevant to decisions affecting employees
compares political institutions, democracy and political behaviour using empirical methods
uses international relations theory and country research to analyse diplomacy, conflicts and institutions
studies EU institutions and policymaking through empirical work on parliamentary amendments
Uses a case study to examine agenda-setting, policy choices and implementation in a global context.
uses sociological theories to investigate institutions, social boundaries and inequality
develops qualitative research through interviews, observation, coding and ethical reflection
studies social movements and environmental justice through cases and perspectives on gender, colonialism and political change
uses social theory and independent research to investigate civil-society organisations and movements
examines neural regulation, sleep, mood and behaviour as biological foundations for psychological health; it is not occupational psychology
introduces psychological and neural explanations of behaviour, learning, personality and mental health
examines social influence, group behaviour and interpersonal processes using psychological research
uses research design and statistical models to analyse and report behavioural findings
examines biopsychosocial explanations of mental disorders and develops evidence appraisal relevant to understanding psychological health
examines stress, health behaviour, health inequalities and interventions as foundations for understanding well-being
develops introductory knowledge of psychological tests, diagnostic interviews and treatments; this is clinical assessment rather than employee selection
develops systematic review and meta-analysis for evidence synthesis in behavioural and health research
examines development, relationships and change across adulthood and later life, providing foundations for thinking about employee development
uses persuasion theory and community projects to study and evaluate communication strategies
blocks: Both address survey design, psychological measurement and analysis; UCR uses leadership and social-experience applications.
Both examine motivation, teams, leadership and organisational culture.
Both introduce sociological theories and apply them to social life.
Both develop qualitative design, data collection and interpretation.
Both examine social influence, group behaviour and social psychological research.
Both develop statistical analysis for social and behavioural data.
Both study stress, health behaviour and well-being; UCR focuses on health and illness more broadly than the workplace.
Both address financial and management-accounting decisions; UCR does not specialise in personnel costs.
Both teach empirical design, operationalisation, measurement and introductory analysis.
Both introduce economic reasoning about markets and economic decisions.
Both address organisational strategy; UCR emphasises digital transformation.

notes.text: Tilburg offers a dedicated sequence in HR strategy, labour law, work and health, personnel assessment, consulting and HR analytics, followed by a required thesis. UCR combines related courses in organisations, psychological health and research, or institutions and policy. Its options do not reproduce the full specialist HRM sequence.
The Tilburg track teaches primarily in Dutch, with some courses in English. UCR teaches in English.

audience.programmeDescription: Human Resource Studies at Tilburg University examines people, work and organisations. It connects personnel policy and organisational performance with employee well-being, drawing on psychology, sociology, management, economics and law.
audience.comparisonExplanation: UCR offers related study through organisations and strategy, psychological health and development, or institutions and policy. Tilburg provides more specialised sequences in HRM, labour law, personnel assessment and people analytics, alongside a required thesis.
